# **Advanced Multi-View Whole-Body Motion Capture Pipeline Design: A 2026 Perspective**

The pursuit of high-fidelity markerless motion capture utilizing sparse, multi-view camera arrays represents one of the most formidable challenges in contemporary computer vision and biomechanical analysis. The specified configuration—three synchronized high-definition cameras positioned at extreme angles including front, rear, and steep top-down overhead within a dome-like setup—introduces severe projective ambiguities. When extracting 133-point whole-body poses for inverse kinematics (IK) retargeting onto advanced game skeletons like the Unreal Engine Manny rig, the reliance on independent, single-frame 2D pose estimators often results in cascading geometric errors. These errors manifest as left/right limb inversion during rear-facing views, catastrophic foreshortening distortions from top-down perspectives, and high-frequency temporal jitter that degrades the final bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) or Filmbox (FBX) animation output. This report provides an exhaustive, rigorously detailed analysis of the state-of-the-art in 2D whole-body pose estimation, multi-view 3D lifting, and temporal smoothing as of mid-2026, architecting an optimal, offline batch-processing pipeline that prioritizes temporal consistency and viewpoint robustness over real-time processing constraints.

## **Geometric and Algorithmic Challenges of the Sparse Dome Setup**

To fully contextualize the performance of modern pose estimators, one must first dissect the geometric realities of the three-camera dome setup. While arrays like the CMU Panoptic Studio utilize hundreds of cameras to achieve dense volumetric reconstruction1, a three-camera system lacks the redundancy required to brute-force depth estimation. The steep overhead camera is particularly problematic; it introduces a near-singularity in the epipolar geometry for vertical movements. From a top-down perspective, a standing human subject appears heavily foreshortened, compressing the spatial variance of the limbs into a highly clustered pixel radius. Traditional 2D pose estimators, trained predominantly on eye-level, front-facing imagery, interpret this clustering as severe occlusion or anatomical deformation, leading to erratic keypoint predictions.  
Similarly, the rear-facing camera introduces severe lateral ambiguity. Without the facial features and chest anatomy to anchor the orientation of the torso, neural networks frequently invert the left and right limbs. When these flawed 2D predictions are fed into a standard algebraic triangulation algorithm, such as the Direct Linear Transformation (DLT), the intersecting rays fail to converge near the true 3D joint center. The resulting high reprojection error causes the 3D joint to "snap" to incorrect local minima across consecutive frames. When this shivering 3D skeleton is retargeted via IK in a game engine, it triggers pole-vector flipping, unnatural bone stretching, and mesh tearing, rendering the animation unusable for professional applications.

## **Evaluation of Viewpoint-Robust 2D Whole-Body Pose Estimators**

The limitations observed in models like CIGPose-X under extreme camera angles stem from the inherent biases of their training paradigms and the algorithmic mechanisms used to handle visual context. To identify the ideal replacement capable of exporting 133 COCO-WholeBody keypoints via ONNX Runtime, it is necessary to rigorously compare the architectural philosophies of the leading models as of 2026: RTMPose/RTMW, DWPose, ViTPose++, Sapiens2, and CIGPose.

### **The Paradox of Causal Intervention in CIGPose**

CIGPose addresses pose estimation robustness by conceptualizing visual context as a confounder within a Structural Causal Model (SCM)3. In highly cluttered environments or under partial occlusion, high-capacity models often rely on superficial statistics rather than true anatomical understanding, spuriously correlating a background object with a human limb. CIGPose identifies this visual context as a confounder that creates a non-causal backdoor path corrupting the model's prediction3. To rectify this, the architecture employs a Causal Intervention Module (CIM) that approximates a true causal intervention. It uses predictive uncertainty to identify confounded keypoint embeddings and replaces them with learned, context-invariant canonical embeddings3. A hierarchical graph neural network then processes these deconfounded embeddings at both local and global semantic levels to enforce anatomical plausibility3.  
While CIGPose-X achieves a highly competitive 67.5% Average Precision (AP) on the COCO-WholeBody dataset when augmented with the UBody dataset3, its reliance on per-frame causal intervention creates a temporal paradox that explains the jitter observed in your current pipeline. Because the identification of confounded features relies on single-frame predictive uncertainty, the intervention threshold may trigger inconsistently across consecutive frames. A leg clearly visible from the top-down camera in one frame might become slightly obscured by the torso in the next, triggering the CIM to suddenly replace the embedding with a canonical prior. This discrete switching behavior creates severe frame-to-frame instability. Furthermore, while the graph neural network enforces local kinematics, it lacks explicit cross-view temporal mechanisms to enforce left/right disambiguation when anatomical priors mirror each other perfectly, as seen in rear-facing silhouettes.

### **Coordinate Classification and Real-Time Architectures: RTMW and DWPose**

RTMW (Real-Time Multi-person Whole-body pose estimation) represents a paradigm shift away from traditional heatmap regression, building upon the highly successful RTMPose architecture5. RTMW is explicitly optimized for 133-point whole-body tracking and employs Simple Coordinate Classification (SimCC)6. Unlike conventional methods that rely on computationally heavy high-resolution heatmaps or direct coordinate regression, SimCC formulates keypoint detection as a classification problem distributed across sub-pixel bins6. This approach preserves fine-grained spatial information while drastically minimizing quantization errors, which are a primary source of micro-jitter in argmax-based heatmap extraction6.  
To handle the immense scale variance between a full torso and tiny finger articulations, RTMW integrates a Part-Aggregation Feature Pyramid Network (PAFPN) and a Hierarchical Encoding Module (HEM) inspired by VQVAE-26. This ensures that the model can resolve the intricate details of the hands and face even when the subject is far from the camera. The RTMW-X variant achieves an unprecedented 70.2 AP on the COCO-WholeBody benchmark, establishing itself as a premier open-source solution5. Crucially for the specified pipeline requirements, RTMW boasts excellent ONNX deployability, natively supporting the onnxruntime-gpu execution provider via the rtmlib implementation, bypassing the complex dependency issues often associated with PyTorch-to-ONNX conversions8.  
DWPose offers a highly efficient alternative within the same architectural family. It functions as a two-stage distilled derivative of RTMPose10. By leveraging a massive teacher model to supervise a lightweight student model via feature-based and logits-based distillation, DWPose maximizes efficiency10. While the DWPose-L model boosted the AP of the baseline RTMPose from 64.8% to 66.5%10, it generally falls slightly short of the sheer representational power of RTMW-X when deployed in offline scenarios where inference speed is secondary to ultimate accuracy. Both models exhibit significantly higher temporal stability than CIGPose due to the continuous nature of their sub-pixel classification mechanisms.

### **Heterogeneous Transformer Scaling in ViTPose++**

ViTPose++ utilizes a plain, non-hierarchical vision transformer backbone, demonstrating the scalability of treating pose estimation as a sequence-to-sequence token problem10. Its primary architectural innovation is knowledge factorization, which employs task-agnostic and task-specific feed-forward networks within the transformer10. This allows the model to deal with heterogeneous body keypoint categories simultaneously, transferring knowledge from massive datasets to smaller, specialized datasets via a simple knowledge token10.  
While ViTPose++ scales exceptionally well to high resolutions (such as 640x480) and offers pristine single-frame accuracy, it remains a purely spatial model. It lacks the inherent multi-view geometric awareness or temporal priors required to resolve the specific rear-view ambiguities present in the target dome setup. Furthermore, its deployment via ONNX can be computationally intensive, often requiring specialized kernel optimizations to achieve reasonable batch processing times compared to the more streamlined CNN-based backbones of RTMW.

### **High-Resolution Foundation Models: Sapiens and Sapiens2**

The Sapiens family of models, particularly the second-generation Sapiens2 released in 2026, represents a brute-force foundation model approach to human-centric vision13. Pretrained via an advanced Masked Autoencoder (MAE) strategy on over one billion carefully curated in-the-wild human images, Sapiens2 operates at a native 1024×768 high resolution, with hierarchical variants supporting up to an astonishing 4K resolution14. The 5-billion parameter Sapiens2-5B model utilizes a joint objective combining masked image reconstruction to preserve low-level fidelity with a global contrastive loss driven by a student-teacher framework based on DINOv314.  
For steep top-down and rear-facing views, Sapiens2 exhibits extraordinary robustness13. The massive pretraining corpus exposes the model to a highly diverse distribution of extreme camera angles, allowing the vision transformer to learn invariant representations of foreshortened limbs that confound lesser models17. Sapiens natively supports a highly dense 308-keypoint topology, but can easily export the required 133 COCO-WholeBody format16. In occlusion cases, Sapiens demonstrates perfect correctness compared to severe failure rates in legacy estimators like OpenPose or OpenPifPaf16.  
However, despite its supremacy in spatial accuracy, Sapiens models present significant deployment friction for ONNX pipelines. The models utilize highly complex transformer blocks, especially the windowed attention mechanisms in the hierarchical 4K variants14. Exporting these dynamic graphs to ONNX for onnxruntime-gpu execution frequently results in unsupported operation errors or drastically degraded inference speeds18. While utility libraries like myogait have emerged to bridge the Sapiens2 PyTorch environment for offline usage9, native ONNX integration remains a critical bottleneck for seamless C++ or C\# game engine ingestion.

## **The Impact of Training Datasets on Viewpoint Invariance**

The performance of a 2D pose estimator is inextricably linked to the statistical variance of its training distribution. The inability of standard models to handle rear-facing and steep overhead views is rarely an architectural flaw, but rather a direct artifact of dataset bias. Understanding the composition of available datasets is paramount for selecting a model capable of parsing the dome setup.  
The standard **COCO-WholeBody** dataset is the foundational benchmark for 133-keypoint estimation19. However, the images are heavily biased toward front-facing, eye-level photography scraped from internet repositories. Models trained exclusively on COCO-WholeBody inherently learn a rigid spatial prior indicating that the human chest, face, and kneecaps are directed toward the camera. This leads directly to the left/right leg disambiguation failures observed when the subject's back is turned, as the network attempts to force the rear-facing silhouette to conform to a front-facing prior.  
The **UBody** dataset addresses specific edge cases by focusing on diverse upper-body scenarios and egocentric perspectives11. Integrating UBody significantly enhances a model's ability to interpret foreshortened arms and unusual framing. This dataset is highly beneficial for mitigating the catastrophic failures associated with the steep overhead camera.  
Most critically for the specified pipeline, the **H3WB (Human3.6M 3D WholeBody)** dataset provides the exact geometric diversity required21. H3WB extends the classic Human3.6M dataset by providing 133 whole-body 2D and 3D annotations across 100,000 images21. Because H3.6M was captured in a highly controlled laboratory environment using a synchronized multi-camera array, the dataset inherently contains mathematically consistent rear, side, and oblique views of every pose21. Models trained on H3WB learn anatomically accurate priors for rear-facing subjects, drastically reducing the incidence of left/right inversion.  
Models utilizing aggressive data-mixing strategies, such as the **Cocktail14** dataset combination used to train RTMW-X, represent the gold standard6. By merging 14 diverse datasets—including COCO-WholeBody, UBody, H3WB, Halpe, and CrowdPose—the resulting model benefits from both the in-the-wild visual diversity of internet scrapes and the mathematical geometric rigor of in-the-lab multi-camera arrays6. The RTMW-X model trained on Cocktail14 is therefore highly recommended, as the H3WB subset explicitly teaches the network how to interpret rear-facing and oblique silhouettes, while the UBody subset aids in resolving the steep top-down perspective20.

## **Imbuing Temporal Consistency: Video-Based Pose Estimation vs. Algorithmic Filtering**

Relying solely on single-frame estimators for motion capture inevitably results in temporally incoherent data. Even with favorable camera angles, algorithmic uncertainty causes keypoint predictions to oscillate within a local pixel radius across consecutive frames. When these jittery 2D coordinates are passed to a 3D triangulation algorithm, the non-linear nature of epipolar geometry amplifies the 2D noise, resulting in violent, high-frequency shivering in the 3D skeleton. This shivering destroys the velocity and acceleration curves required for smooth IK retargeting, resulting in robotic, erratic game animation.

### **Video-Based Spatiotemporal Neural Networks**

To address this at the network level, video-based pose estimation frameworks extend the 2D architecture across the temporal dimension. Frameworks like **PAVE-Net** eliminate heuristic operations such as Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) and RoI cropping, providing a fully end-to-end framework for multi-person video pose estimation24. By utilizing a novel pose-aware attention mechanism, PAVE-Net matches pose queries to features across consecutive frames, explicitly modeling spatiotemporal dependencies among both human instances and fine-grained body keypoints24.  
Similarly, sequence-based transformer models like **SeqFormer** and **TCFormer** leverage temporal self-attention to smooth predictions natively25. The network analyzes a sliding window of frames to predict the pose at the current timestep. If an arm is heavily foreshortened in the top-down view at a specific frame, the temporal attention mechanism retrieves the arm's trajectory from the preceding and succeeding frames, successfully interpolating the position and neutralizing single-frame geometric failures. While highly effective, these spatiotemporal models often require complex custom ONNX graph constructions to manage the temporal buffer states, complicating offline batch pipelines.

### **Algorithmic Post-Processing: Savitzky-Golay vs. OneEuro**

For offline batch processing where the entire motion sequence is available, applying rigorous mathematical filtering to the 2D tracks post-inference is often vastly more efficient and reliable than deploying heavy spatiotemporal neural networks.  
While the **OneEuro filter** is ubiquitous in real-time applications because it dynamically adjusts its cutoff frequency based on movement speed to balance jitter reduction and latency, it is suboptimal for offline processing. For batch processing where future frames are accessible, the **Savitzky-Golay (S-G) filter** provides vastly superior trajectory smoothing27.  
The S-G filter operates by sliding a window of fixed size (e.g., ![][image1] frames) over the coordinate data and fitting a low-degree polynomial to the points within the window using the method of linear least squares28. The smoothed coordinate ![][image2] at frame ![][image3] is the value of the fitted polynomial evaluated at the center of the window. The mathematical formulation seeks to minimize the sum of the squared errors:

where ![][image5] represents the raw 2D coordinate from the neural network, ![][image6] is the polynomial degree, and ![][image7] are the calculated coefficients28.  
Unlike simple moving averages or median filters which blunt the peaks of rapid movements (such as a fast punch, a sudden jump, or an abrupt stop), the S-G filter impeccably preserves the high-frequency anatomical features of the motion curve28. Applying an S-G filter with a window size of 11 to 15 frames and a polynomial order of 3 independently to the X and Y coordinates of the 2D tracks prior to 3D lifting will dramatically stabilize the resulting 3D geometry, removing the neural network noise while maintaining the biomechanical fidelity of the actor's performance28.

## **Transcending Triangulation: Advanced Multi-View 2D-to-3D Lifting**

The traditional approach to multi-camera motion capture involves detecting 2D keypoints in each view and projecting them into 3D space using algebraic triangulation, typically via Direct Linear Transformation (DLT). However, in a sparse three-camera dome setup with highly disparate angles, DLT is highly vulnerable to catastrophic failure.  
Algebraic triangulation assumes that the 2D keypoint in the front camera corresponds to the exact same anatomical sub-surface as the keypoint in the rear camera. In reality, a 2D network might predict the "left shoulder" on the front of the deltoid in the front camera, but on the back of the deltoid in the rear camera. When triangulated, these slightly offset rays do not intersect perfectly. DLT attempts to find the midpoint of the shortest line segment connecting these non-intersecting rays, resulting in a distorted 3D joint that drifts rapidly as the subject moves. To resolve this, the research community has shifted decisively toward deep learning-based multi-view 3D lifting and volumetric fusion models.

### **Volumetric and Cross-View Fusion Mechanisms**

Methods such as **VoxelKeypointFusion** and **RapidPoseTriangulation** completely abandon direct 2D ray intersection31. Instead, they project the 2D joint heatmaps or coordinate confidence values from all available views into a shared, discretized 3D voxelized bounding volume representing the capture space32. The intersection of these projections creates dense 3D probability clouds. A 3D Convolutional Neural Network—or a computationally lighter 2D projection equivalent like Faster-VoxelPose—then processes this volumetric data to regress the final 3D joint centers31. This volumetric approach is inherently robust to calibration noise and minor 2D localization errors, as the network learns the spatial prior of the human skeleton and forces the 3D output to conform to valid anatomical constraints36.  
**AdaPose3D** addresses the specific challenge of the steep top-down camera by actively managing cross-view scale inconsistency38. Perspective variations cause massive discrepancies in the perceived size of limbs across the three views. AdaPose3D dynamically adjusts the Gaussian kernel sizes of the heatmaps based on the perspective projection, ensuring that the feature fusion remains consistent and properly weighted despite the extreme angle differences38.

### **Transformer-Based Hypothesis Generation and State Space Models**

**MHFormer (Multi-Hypothesis Transformer)** approaches the depth ambiguity problem by explicitly generating multiple feasible 3D pose hypotheses from the 2D data39. It acknowledges that a noisy 2D input from a heavily foreshortened overhead camera could mathematically correspond to several valid 3D leg positions. The network generates multiple hypotheses, allows them to communicate via a hypothesis-mixing Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to share spatial context, and synthesizes a final, highly accurate 3D pose by converging the hypotheses39.  
**MotionBERT** utilizes a sophisticated Dual-Stream Spatial-Temporal Transformer (DSTformer)41. By processing a sequence of 2D poses rather than a single frame, MotionBERT leverages both spatial structural priors and long-range temporal motion priors. It is exceptionally capable of smoothing out severe tracking losses in individual cameras, relying on the temporal stream to hallucinate missing data in an anatomically realistic manner based on the trajectory of the movement41.  
Emerging in 2025 and 2026, **MV-SSM (Multi-View State Space Modeling)** represents the integration of Mamba-style state space models into 3D multi-view geometry43. By explicitly modeling the joint spatial sequences at both the feature level from multi-view images and the person keypoint level, MV-SSM harnesses the sequence-modeling strengths of state space models to predict 3D human keypoints with unprecedented efficiency, excelling in scenarios with significant self-occlusions43.

### **Ray-Based Universal Multi-View Lifting (RUMPL)**

The most advanced and highly recommended approach for the specified dome setup is **RUMPL (Ray-Based Transformers for Universal Multi-View 2D to 3D Human Pose Lifting)**44. Traditional neural lifting models must be trained on specific multi-view datasets (like H3.6M) and implicitly memorize the laboratory's exact camera calibration. If the user's dome cameras are placed slightly differently than the training data, the model fails to generalize44.  
RUMPL elegantly bypasses this limitation by operating entirely in 3D ray space rather than 2D image space. The 2D pixel keypoints ![][image8] (in homogeneous coordinates) are converted into normalized camera coordinates by applying the inverse of the intrinsic matrix ![][image9]46:  
![][image10]  
The network then computes the direction of each ray in the world referential originating from the camera center by multiplying by the transposed rotation matrix ![][image11]:  
![][image12]  
Each keypoint is then mathematically represented as a 3D ray ![][image13], concatenating the camera translation location ![][image14] with the direction vector ![][image15]46.  
These 3D rays from all three cameras are fed as sequence tokens into a View Fusion Transformer44. Because the input is a set of geometric rays rather than coordinate pixels, RUMPL is entirely agnostic to the number of cameras or their extreme angles. The self-attention mechanism evaluates the geometric proximity of the rays and cross-references them against learned 3D skeletal priors. If the top-down camera provides a wildly incorrect, foreshortened 2D prediction for a leg, its 3D ray will diverge significantly from the rays generated by the front and rear cameras. The View Fusion Transformer will assign a low attention weight to the erroneous top-down ray and rely on the intersection of the front and rear rays, guided by the structural prior of human femur length. RUMPL significantly outperforms standard algebraic triangulation, reducing Mean Per Joint Position Error (MPJPE) by over 50%, and natively exports clean, 3D anatomical structures ideal for IK solving44.

## **Optimal 2026 Pipeline Architecture for Mocap to Game Animation**

Based on the synthesis of current computer vision research, the specific geometric constraints of the three-camera dome setup, and the objective of exporting flawlessly clean BVH/FBX data for the Unreal Engine Manny skeleton, the following architectural pipeline is recommended.

### **Stage 1: High-Resolution Viewpoint-Robust 2D Detection**

Retain **YOLOX-Nano** for initial bounding box detection, ensuring tight crops around the subject. Replace the unstable CIGPose-X model with **RTMW-X** (Real-Time Multi-person Whole-body), configured for a high input resolution of 512x384 or 640x480. RTMW-X is chosen because it natively outputs the required 133 COCO-WholeBody keypoints, utilizes SimCC sub-pixel classification for inherent spatial stability, and is flawlessly deployable via ONNX Runtime for GPU acceleration6. Crucially, the model deployed must be the variant pretrained on the **Cocktail14** dataset combination9. The deep integration of H3WB and UBody data guarantees that RTMW-X possesses the structural priors necessary to accurately parse the rear-facing and steep overhead camera views without suffering from left/right limb inversion or foreshortening collapse.

### **Stage 2: Offline Temporal Conditioning**

Rather than deploying complex video-based RNNs or temporal transformers that unnecessarily complicate the ONNX pipeline, perform mathematical filtering on the extracted 2D coordinate tracks. Apply a **Savitzky-Golay filter** across the temporal axis for each of the ![][image16] (X,Y) coordinate streams independently for each camera view27. Utilizing a window size of 11 to 15 frames with a 3rd-order polynomial will eliminate the high-frequency jitter associated with sub-pixel neural network noise while flawlessly preserving the velocity peaks and precise timings of dynamic actions28. This ensures that the inputs to the 3D lifting stage are mathematically smooth trajectories rather than discrete, noisy points.

### **Stage 3: Ray-Based 3D Lifting**

Completely discard naive algebraic Direct Linear Transformation (DLT) triangulation. Transform the temporally smoothed 2D keypoints into 3D world-space rays using the carefully calibrated intrinsic and extrinsic matrices of the three dome cameras46. Pass these continuous ray vectors into the **RUMPL** View Fusion Transformer44.  
RUMPL will aggregate the rays, heavily discounting the unavoidable foreshortened errors from the top-down camera through its dynamic attention mechanism, and output a clean, anatomically constrained 3D point cloud44. Because RUMPL is trained on synthetic ray intersections with simulated detector noise, it acts as a secondary layer of structural smoothing. It guarantees that bone lengths remain rigidly constant throughout the motion sequence, a critical biomechanical requirement for preventing mesh tearing during game engine retargeting.

### **Stage 4: IK Retargeting and Output Generation**

The stabilized 133-point 3D skeleton—encompassing the 17 core body joints, 6 foot joints, dense hand articulations, and facial landmarks—is mapped to the Unreal Engine Manny control rig. Because the 3D coordinate data generated by the RUMPL lifting stage maintains strict temporal consistency and rigid bone-length constraints, the IK solver will function optimally, free from the pole-vector flipping artifacts that occur when jittery knees or elbows rapidly cross the IK plane threshold. The resulting animation can be seamlessly baked down to the target skeleton and exported via batch script to FBX or BVH formats, delivering professional-grade motion capture fidelity from a highly constrained sparse camera array.
